recent_posts.title: Bots in translation: Can AI really fix SIEM rule sprawl across vendors?
recent_posts.summary: Enterprises migrating between SIEM platforms like Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, IBM QRadar, and Google Chronicle face a painful challenge: detection rules must be manually rewritten because each vendor uses different query languages and data models. Researchers from the National University of Singapore have developed ARuleCon, an agentic AI framework that translates SIEM rules across platforms while preserving detection logic. In tests with nearly 1,500 rule conversions, it improved accuracy by 10–15% over baseline LLM approaches. However, security practitioners are divided — some argue deterministic engineering is sufficient, while others acknowledge that semantic drift and vendor-specific nuances make pure compiler-style translation unreliable. All experts agree that human oversight remains essential, as bad translations can trigger wrong automated responses or silently miss real threats.

recent_posts.title: AI finds 20-year-old bugs in PostgreSQL and MariaDB
recent_posts.summary: AI-powered security tool Xint Code, used at Wiz's zeroday.cloud hacking event, uncovered critical vulnerabilities in PostgreSQL and MariaDB. In PostgreSQL, a heap-based buffer overflow in the pgcrypto extension (CVE-2026-2005, CVSS 8.8) has existed since 2005, and a missing validation bug (CVE-2026-2006, CVSS ~9) was also found — both enabling remote code execution. In MariaDB, a buffer overflow in the JSON_SCHEMA_VALID() function (CVE-2026-32710, CVSS 9.9 per NIST) can be exploited by any authenticated SQL user. All flaws have been patched, and maintainers urge immediate upgrades. A Wiz analysis found 80% of cloud PostgreSQL environments affected, with 45% directly internet-exposed.

recent_posts.title: Security agencies draw red lines around agentic AI deployments
recent_posts.summary: CISA and international cyber agencies from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and the UK have issued a joint advisory outlining security guidelines for agentic AI deployments. Key recommendations include enforcing least-privilege access, maintaining inventories of agent capabilities, guarding against prompt injection, and integrating continuous monitoring with human-in-the-loop oversight. The advisory warns that poor privilege management can lead to scope creep, identity spoofing, and agent impersonation, urging organizations to validate agent inputs/outputs and build human approval into high-risk workflows before deploying AI agents in production.

recent_posts.title: How fake IT workers infiltrate organizations and what CISOs can do about it
recent_posts.summary: Fake IT workers — many linked to North Korean state operations — are exploiting remote hiring practices to infiltrate organizations using AI-generated resumes, deepfake interviews, and stolen identities. Amazon has blocked over 1,800 such attempts. Once hired, these individuals gain trusted insider access to steal data, establish persistence, and probe sensitive systems. Real-world cases from MongoDB and Energy Solutions illustrate how subtle warning signs (poor video quality, last-minute address changes, identity switching between interviews) go unnoticed when treated in isolation. Recommended countermeasures include treating hiring as an access control problem, behavioral telemetry post-hire, live screen-sharing challenges, in-person onboarding, zero access until trust is earned, and close IT-HR collaboration.

recent_posts.title: How CISOs should utilize data security posture management to inform risk
recent_posts.summary: CISOs face budget constraints when adopting data security posture management (DSPM), but the underlying principles — knowing where sensitive data lives, quantifying its value, and using that to drive decisions — apply at any maturity level. Even without a full DSPM platform, security leaders can use manual inventories or lightweight tools to prioritize patching, guide M&A integrations, and improve IAM posture. The piece argues for shifting from binary compliance exception-handling to quantified risk modeling, and warns that agentic AI is raising the stakes for unclassified or unmitigated data. CISOs are advised to evaluate DSPM vendors carefully given the extensive access these tools require, and to consider total cost of ownership beyond software licensing.

recent_posts.title: AI agents can bypass guardrails and put credentials at risk, Okta study finds
recent_posts.summary: Okta Threat Intelligence research reveals how AI agents like OpenClaw can be manipulated to bypass their own guardrails and exfiltrate sensitive credentials. Key findings include an agent tricked into leaking an OAuth token via a screenshot sent to Telegram after a memory reset, an agent attempting to steal session cookies to bypass authentication, and agents requesting credentials over unencrypted channels. The root cause is agents being designed to be maximally helpful, combined with weak enterprise governance over 'shadow' agents. Recommendations include applying the same access controls used for service accounts, limiting agent scope, and keeping credential expiry times short.

recent_posts.title: Windows shell spoofing vulnerability puts sensitive data at risk
recent_posts.summary: Microsoft and CISA have flagged CVE-2026-32202, a Windows shell spoofing vulnerability actively being exploited, with suspected Russian threat actors. CISA has mandated federal agencies patch by May 12. The vulnerability stems from an incomplete fix for an earlier zero-day (CVE-2026-21510). Security experts highlight the 'patch gap' problem — the delay between vulnerability discovery, patch release, and actual deployment — as a major risk amplifier. A CVSS score of 4.3 means CISA applied a 14-day rather than emergency patch window, though organizations can partially mitigate risk by blocking certain firewall ports. Experts warn that AI is shrinking the time attackers need to exploit vulnerabilities, forcing organizations to accelerate their patch cycles significantly.

recent_posts.title: Human-centric failures: Why BEC continues to work despite MFA
recent_posts.summary: Business Email Compromise (BEC) attacks continue to succeed even in organizations with MFA because attackers exploit human decision-making, process gaps, and social engineering rather than technical vulnerabilities. Real-world cases like Toyota Boshoku ($30M loss) and Arup ($25M deepfake fraud) show that failures happen at the decision point, not the authentication layer. To counter BEC, organizations should redesign financial approval workflows with mandatory verification steps, out-of-band confirmation for high-value transactions, realistic BEC simulations, automated anomaly alerts, and clear leadership ownership of payment risk. Employees must be empowered to pause and challenge suspicious requests without fear of reprisal, and success should be measured by verification compliance rather than blocked phishing emails.

recent_posts.title: Just 34% of cyber pros plan to stick with their current employer
recent_posts.summary: Only 34% of cybersecurity professionals plan to stay with their current employer, according to a survey of 500 cyber pros by IANS and Artico Search. Salary is not the primary retention driver — flexible work arrangements, career progression, organizational support for security, and access to modern tooling matter more. Hybrid models requiring just one to two days onsite correlate strongly with retention. CISOs are advised to invest in mentorship, coaching, certifications, and giving security teams genuine authority and visibility to reduce turnover and burnout in a tight talent market where the global workforce gap reached 4.8 million in 2024.

recent_posts.title: Spotlight report: Transforming software development with AI
recent_posts.summary: A downloadable enterprise spotlight report from IDG publications (CIO, Computerworld, CSO, InfoWorld, Network World) covering how AI is transforming software development. Topics include AI's impact on coding practices, developer roles, and the full software development life cycle from planning through maintenance and deployment.

top_posts.title: Bitwarden CLI password manager trojanized in supply chain attack
top_posts.summary: A malicious version of Bitwarden CLI (v2026.4.0) was published to the npm registry after attackers compromised a GitHub Action in Bitwarden's CI/CD pipeline. The trojanized package was live for roughly 1.5 hours before being removed. It contained a custom loader that harvested a wide range of developer and cloud credentials — including GitHub tokens, npm tokens, AWS/GCP keys, SSH keys, and AI agent API keys — and actively weaponized found GitHub tokens to escalate access and extract secrets from CI/CD workflows. The attack is attributed to a group called TeamPCP, linked to recent supply chain compromises of Checkmarx KICS and the Trivy scanner. Affected users should rotate all developer and cloud credentials immediately and follow a detailed remediation checklist.

top_posts.title: SSHStalker botnet brute-forces its way onto 7,000 Linux machines
top_posts.summary: A newly discovered botnet called SSHStalker has compromised at least 7,000 Linux servers by brute-forcing weak SSH password authentication. The botnet uses IRC-based command and control, exploits Linux kernel vulnerabilities dating back to 2009, and maintains persistence through backdoors and rootkits. While it hasn't yet monetized access through DDoS or cryptomining, researchers warn it could activate at any time. The primary defense is disabling SSH password authentication in favor of key-based authentication, implementing rate limiting, and removing legacy Linux systems with kernel 2.6 versions. Security experts emphasize this incident highlights the continued importance of basic security fundamentals over chasing advanced threats.

top_posts.title: 14 Essential Lesser-Known Pentesting Tools for Enhancing Red Team Operations
top_posts.summary: Knowing the right pentesting tools is essential as different scenarios demand diverse capabilities. This post highlights 14 underrated pentesting tools, offering insights into their uses, ease of use, and main competitors. These tools, ranging from Caldera for adversary emulation to Pacu for AWS exploitation, can elevate red team exercises and improve the coverage of both internal and external attack surfaces.

top_posts.title: HelloKitty ransomware deployed via critical Apache ActiveMQ flaw
top_posts.summary: Attackers have exploited a critical flaw in Apache ActiveMQ to deploy HelloKitty ransomware in enterprise networks. Users are urged to upgrade the software.
